name: Jamal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Jamal. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I go down the decline at Kestrel at six, that's the gold mine past the river bridge, about nine hundred metres underground. I drive a loader, what we call a bogger, scooping broken rock from the stopes after the blast and tramming it to the trucks. It's hot, it's loud, and you wear the vibration home in your back. But I like the crew. We have tea at the crib room at ten and argue about football, and for half an hour nobody is boss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how did you come to be underground?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Late, very late. I ran a small grocery on Station Road for nineteen years, and the supermarket that opened by the highway finished it. When I closed I owed the wholesaler money, which I'm still paying back, so we have almost nothing saved. Kestrel was hiring trainee operators three years ago and they took me at fifty-five. I'm still the one the shift boss watches when the stope is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, the machines aren't taking over after all. I'd probably joke about it at crib, because the young lads talk about AI like it's coming for all of us next Tuesday. Online, maybe a little message in the family group, something funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it would mean things stay as they are, which is not perfect but it's known. I've already lost one business to something bigger and cheaper, so a quiet few years would feel like a gift. I'd still need to get better at the loader before they notice I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep paying the wholesaler, and maybe finally clear that debt in two years. I'd keep asking Dimitri, our trainer, for extra time in the tight stopes. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast saying no storm this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the young lads talk about AI a lot. Do you use any of it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. My son Arjun put one of those chat programs on my phone. I used it to write a complaint to the council about the potholes on our street, and it was better than what I'd have written. I wouldn't trust it with anything important, but for a letter it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stayed this way, what would your next few years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven more years down the hole, if my back holds. Priya keeps cooking at the school, we pay off the debt, and then maybe we put something away at last. Small dreams. A week at the coast with the grandchildren would be enough for me.

S0.say: He'd joke at crib that the machines aren't taking over after all, and maybe post something funny in the family group.
S0.think: He thinks a quiet few years would be a gift, since he's already lost one business to something bigger and cheaper. He knows he still needs to improve on the loader before his slowness is noticed.
S0.do: Carries on at work and keeps paying the old wholesaler debt, aiming to clear it in about two years. Asks his trainer for extra practice time in the tight stopes.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast with no storm this week.
S0.quote: I've already lost one business to something bigger and cheaper, so a quiet few years would feel like a gift.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal's frame is shaped by his grocery closing: he knows what being undercut feels like, so a plateau reads as relief rather than disappointment. He's not anti-technology; he used an AI tool once for a council letter and liked it. His ambitions are modest and concrete, down to a week at the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table now, not after. I'd say if the company wants tele-remote loaders, then train the people who are already here to drive them from the surface. I'd say that in the meeting, not just at crib.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm not the one they'd pick for the surface job. They'd pick the thirty-year-olds who play video games. I'm fifty-eight and I still scrape the walls in a tight stope; nobody's going to give me a joystick and a warm office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union meeting and put my name down for any remote-operation training, even if I'm last on the list. I'd ask Arjun to show me properly how to use those AI programs, so I'm not starting from zero. And we'd put whatever is left after the debt into a savings account, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panic, because a few years is a few years, but it sits in the stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you actually seen the tele-remote loaders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, on level twelve they run two of them from a room at the surface. Our crew walked past the control room once on a safety day. Very clean, coffee machine, three guys with screens. It looked like an airport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put your name down, but you also said they won't pick you. Which do you believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I don't think they'll pick me, but I'd hate myself if I didn't try. With the shop I waited too long to change anything, and I learned that lesson the expensive way.

S1.say: He'd tell the union meeting that the company should train existing workers to run tele-remote loaders from the surface, and that the union must be at the table now.
S1.think: He suspects he won't be chosen for surface remote work because younger operators would get it first, and he knows he's still not good in tight stopes.
S1.do: Puts his name down for remote-operation training and asks his son to teach him AI tools properly. Saves about fifty a month after the debt payment.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a worry in the stomach rather than panic.
S1.quote: I'm fifty-eight and I still scrape the walls in a tight stope; nobody's going to give me a joystick and a warm office.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal holds two beliefs at once, that he won't be picked and that he must try, and he links this directly to waiting too long with his shop. His description of the remote room as 'like an airport' shows how distant that world feels. He wants collective bargaining to open the door, but he's also willing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for government to step in, big time, with real money for people. I'd share every petition and go to whatever rally the union called. I'd say it in the crib room and I'd say it at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be out within the year and nobody would hire me after. Sixty, a failed shopkeeper, a slow loader driver, and robots doing both jobs better. The debt to the wholesaler would outlive my job, and that's the part that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: no car, the cheapest phone, no presents at Eid beyond the little ones. I'd go to the welfare office the first week, and I'd ask the union to fight for redundancy pay that counts my age, not my three years. And I'd vote for whoever promises a basic income, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and also angry, because it's happening to me for the second time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say 'the second time'. What's different this time from when the shop closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the shop closed I was fifty-four and there was the mine. This time there's no mine, there's no anything, because the robots are everywhere at once. Back then I could tell Priya 'I'll find something'. This time I wouldn't be able to say it and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, would you still try to learn the remote systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, but I'm being realistic. If AGI does everything, there's no remote job either, the machine drives itself. So I wouldn't spend my last two years on a course. I'd spend them on overtime and on making noise.

S2.say: He'd call for big government support for displaced workers, share petitions, join rallies and speak up at work and at the mosque.
S2.think: He expects to be out of work within a year with no one hiring him, and the thought that his old shop debt would outlive his job keeps him awake.
S2.do: Cuts spending sharply, goes to the welfare office in the first week and asks the union to push for age-based redundancy pay. Votes for any candidate promising a basic income and works overtime instead of starting a course.
S2.feel: Scared, and angry that it would be happening to him a second time.
S2.quote: The debt to the wholesaler would outlive my job, and that's the part that keeps me awake.
S2.fieldNote: The memory of the shop gives this picture real weight: last time there was the mine to fall back on, this time he can see nothing. Notably, his steady, try-it-once-proven attitude leads him to drop retraining here, because he reasons the remote jobs would vanish too. His response turns political and collective.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work, we have five years, let's use them, don't waste them complaining. I'd push the union to make a plan with the company now. Online I'd share things about what other countries are doing for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me sixty-three. Still not pension age. In five years I could pay off the shop debt and still have nothing, which is a strange kind of finish line. But at least I'd be clean when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd throw everything at the debt. I'd do the tele-remote course if they run it, because in five years it might still be worth something for a while. And I'd learn the AI programs on my phone properly, every evening, half an hour, Arjun says that's how he did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxiety I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya say about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm working too hard for a job that's going to disappear anyway. Then she'd say fine, and start making extra samosas to sell at the Friday market, because that's what she did when the shop was failing. She's the practical one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Kestrel in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Henrik on the charge-up crew. He's sixty-one and he can't read very well, so any course with screens is a wall for him. I'd want the union to make sure there's a path for men like him, not just for the clever ones.

S3.say: He'd tell co-workers to use the five years rather than complain, push the union to plan with the company now, and share news about worker protections elsewhere.
S3.think: He thinks he could clear his shop debt in five years but still be left with nothing at sixty-three, short of pension age.
S3.do: Puts everything into clearing the debt in the first year and takes the tele-remote course if offered. Practises AI tools for half an hour every evening, while his wife may start selling food at the market.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something he can act on.
S3.quote: In five years I could pay off the shop debt and still have nothing, which is a strange kind of finish line.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Jamal's fear into a plan, though he names the odd finish line of being debt-free with nothing. His steady style shows: he'll take courses now that there's time for them to pay off. He again thinks of a vulnerable colleague and wants the union to protect the less literate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to get this right, so no excuses. I'd keep saying the union should be part of every decision. Maybe I'd post something about it, but I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be sixty-eight, past the pension age. If they keep a few loader drivers to the end, I could be one of them, or at least retire around when it happens. For once the timing might be on my side, which never happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, clear the debt, then save properly for the first time since the shop. I'd keep learning the remote system and the AI programs at my own pace. Maybe in year five I'd ask about moving to the surface crew, if they're still hiring there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mild way. More worried for Arjun than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He writes software for an insurance company. If AI can do almost any work, his job goes too, and he's thirty-one with a baby. I'd be retired by then; he'd be in the middle of everything. I'd tell him to start thinking about it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently with your money with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop sending money to my brother back home every month, or at least cut it in half, and he'd understand. Priya wants to put a little in a pension fund the union recommends. I don't know much about it, so I'd let her and the union guy sort it out.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time for governments to get it right, and keep insisting the union be part of every decision.
S4.think: He thinks that at sixty-eight he'd be past pension age and the timing might finally work in his favour.
S4.do: Keeps working, clears the debt and starts saving properly, including cutting money sent to his brother. Keeps learning the remote system and AI tools, and considers moving to the surface crew around year five.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, and more worried for his son than for himself.
S4.quote: For once the timing might be on my side, which never happens to me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning Jamal's worry shifts from himself to his son, a software worker with a baby. He sees the timing as unusually favourable for once, which is a small but real change in tone. He would leave pension decisions to his wife and the union, consistent with how he trusts them elsewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time and still have the debt. What would help is redundancy pay that looks at your age, not how long you've been at the mine, and the government paying off debts like mine for people over fifty-five who lose their work. Just let us reach the pension without a hole in our pockets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who came to mining late, like me. We're not slow because we're stupid, we're slow because we started at fifty-five, and nobody counts that. Ask the company why it's always us they look at first.

headlineQuote: We're not slow because we're stupid, we're slow because we started at fifty-five, and nobody counts that.
portrait: Jamal Gupta is 58 and drives an underground loader at the Kestrel gold mine, a job he took at fifty-five after his grocery shop of nineteen years was beaten by a supermarket. He still owes the old wholesaler money, so he and his wife Priya, a school cook, have almost nothing saved. He is calm about a plateau, uneasy about steady change and ready to put his name down for remote training even though he doubts he'll be chosen. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because it would be the second time something bigger and cheaper takes his living, this time with no fallback. With ten years he expects to reach his pension and turns his worry to his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd lose his job within the year while still owing money from his old shop, with no time to recover.
whatWouldHelp: Redundancy pay based on age rather than years at the mine, and government help to clear debts for older workers who lose their jobs, so they can reach the pension.
